title: Loading and skeletons on a marketing site
excerpt: A marketing page should arrive with the offer already rendered. Fix the wait before you design a skeleton, and keep placeholders for true empty states.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. The ready desk fits a piece about pages that should arrive already filled in.
caption: The page should be ready when the visitor is. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a marketing page use a skeleton screen?
faqs.answer: Usually no. The headline, the offer, and the way to talk to you can be in the first HTML response. A skeleton means the browser is waiting on data the page could have sent already. Fix that wait, then see if any placeholder is still needed.

faqs.question: When is a skeleton honest?
faqs.answer: It is honest when the layout is stable and the missing part is truly unknown at request time, such as a signed-in name or a live inventory count on an otherwise static page. It is not honest as a costume for a slow hero image or a font that blocks the sentence. web.dev treats loading, response, and visual stability as separate problems, and a gray box can fail all three.

faqs.question: What should I ask a studio to show me?
faqs.answer: Ask to load the homepage on a phone, on a slow connection, with the cache cleared. You should see the offer, not a full-page shimmer. Ask which element is the largest content, and whether its space is reserved so the page does not jump. Ask for the version that still makes sense if the extra data never arrives.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A marketing page should not introduce itself as a set of gray blocks. If you are looking at a skeleton screen marketing site, the page is waiting on something it should have rendered. Fix the wait. Design a placeholder only after the wait is gone and something on the page is still, truly, unknown.

The homepage, the offer, the proof, and the way to book a conversation are known before anyone arrives. They can be HTML. A shimmer over that content tells the buyer the site is thinking about a sentence you already wrote.

## The page should already be the page

A company site is not a feed. You are not fetching a timeline that changes every second. You are showing a decision: what you do, who it is for, and how to talk. That decision can ship in the document the server sends. The visitor's first paint can be the headline.

Treat a full-page skeleton as a bug report. Something in the chain is late. A client-side request for copy that lives in the repository. A hero image with no reserved space and no sensible size. A font that hides the text until it arrives. A tag manager that must run before the button exists. Each of these can be moved so the offer shows up first.

Next.js can render a marketing route as HTML before the browser does extra work. React still handles the parts that change. TypeScript keeps the props of a page honest so a missing field fails in development instead of becoming a blank band in production. The stack is a means. The result the founder should see is a page that reads on first paint.

If a section depends on a CMS draft, publish the stable version and let editors change it later. Do not hold the public page hostage to a round trip that could have been done at build time. Vercel will serve that rendered page from the edge. The skeleton is what you get when the render was postponed until the stranger showed up.

## What the gray boxes are saying

A skeleton promises that a specific shape is about to fill in. That promise is useful inside a product, where the layout is known and the records are not. A list of messages can show ten rows of the right height while the records arrive. The person already knows they are in the inbox.

On a marketing page the person does not know the shape of your argument yet. Gray bars do not explain the product. They delay the explanation and they look like every other app that loaded slowly last week. The brand difference you paid for is invisible during the only seconds that decide whether they stay.

There is a second message, and it is worse. A skeleton that never resolves, or resolves into a different layout, teaches people not to trust the first screen. They wait to click. They wait to read. You designed a pause into the sale.

If the placeholder animates, you have also asked the phone to paint a loop before it paints the offer. That work competes with the tap on the booking link. The page feels busy and empty at the same time.

## The waits that are real

Some waits are honest. A search results page does not know the query until the person types it. A filtered catalog on a large store may need a moment after a choice. A portal that shows that client's files cannot invent the files in the public HTML. Those are product moments. A skeleton, or a quieter pending state, can belong there if the frame stays still.

A marketing page rarely has that excuse. The founder already approved the headline. The photographs already exist. The form fields are the same for every visitor. Rendering them on the server is the straightforward path. Reaching for a skeleton means the build treated the brochure like a dashboard.

Third-party widgets are the usual leak. A chat bubble, a review embed, an A/B script, a calendar iframe that loads in the hero. Each one can delay the sentence or shove it down after the fact. Put widgets below the offer, or load them after the page is usable. The hero is not a slot for other companies' JavaScript.

Fonts are the quieter leak. A custom face that blocks rendering will leave the skeleton, or a blank header, in charge. Use a fallback that has similar metrics, and let the type swap without rearranging the lines. The brand font can arrive. It should not be a gate.

## Loading, response, and a page that stays still

web.dev defines three Core Web Vitals that map cleanly onto this mistake. Largest Contentful Paint should happen within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load, at the 75th percentile, looked at separately on mobile and desktop. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should be 0.1 or less. A skeleton often delays the largest element, burns time on the main thread, and then shifts when the real content replaces the bars.

Google's documentation on Core Web Vitals treats those same loading, interaction, and stability signals as part of page experience in search. A passing score is not the goal of the homepage. A readable offer is. The numbers are how you notice that the gray boxes are doing harm a founder can feel without a chart.

Reserve space for anything that arrives late. If an image is the largest element, give it width and height so the headline does not jump when it lands. If you truly need a pending state, match its box to the final box. A short bar that becomes three paragraphs is a layout shift with a costume.

Measure on a phone. A laptop on the office network will hide the skeleton entirely, or show it for a blink you never count. The buyer on a train will see the blink as the whole page. Ask for the slow run, not the demo run.

## Empty is not the same as loading

An empty state is what a person sees when there is nothing to show: no search hits, no open roles, no files in the portal yet. It should say so, and say what to do. A skeleton that shimmers over an empty collection pretends the data is coming. That is a different bug. Stop the animation and write the sentence.

Loading is a temporary status. Empty is an answer. Error is a third answer. The copy for each one is short and different. "Loading projects" on a marketing page that has three case studies in the repository is the wrong sentence. "No roles are open" on a careers page is the right kind of sentence, and it does not need a pulse.

If a section fails to fetch, show the rest of the page. A hero that depends on a single request will take the whole visit down with it. The offer, the navigation, and the contact path should survive a failed extra. Degrade to the words. The words were always the point.

## What to remove before anyone draws a placeholder

Make a list of what the first screen needs. Usually it is the navigation, the headline, one paragraph, one picture, and one action. Confirm each of those can be in the initial HTML. Then time a cold load on a mid-range phone. If the offer is readable at once, you do not have a skeleton project. You have a page.

If something is still late, name it. A four-thousand-pixel image in a small column. A video background. A script in the head. Fix that thing. Designing a more beautiful shimmer is a way of accepting the delay as a feature. It is not a feature. It is a tax on the buyer.

Keep motion off the waiting state. A still, correctly sized box is easier to replace without a jump, and it respects people who asked the system for less motion. The marketing site can still have one considered animation where it explains a change. It does not need a loading costume.

When the page is this simple, the review is simple too. Read it. Tap the action. Confirm nothing jumps. If you cannot do those three things immediately, the skeleton is a symptom and the page is late.

Write the pending state as a sentence when you do need one. "Checking availability" next to a date field tells the truth. A full-screen shimmer does not. Keep that sentence in the same type as the form, and keep the rest of the form usable while it shows. People can review what they already typed. They should not lose the field under an animation.

If two templates share a layout, share the rule. The homepage, the article, and the contact page should all paint their own words first. A skeleton component copied into every route will spread the delay as a house style. Delete the component when the last honest use is gone. A design system is allowed to get smaller.

If you want a second pair of eyes on a page that should arrive already written, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the URL and the slow-phone recording. The useful conversation is about what the first response contains.

A banner that arrives late and covers the headline is the next way a ready page gets interrupted. [Cookie banners that do not cover the offer](/blog/cookie-banners-that-do-not-cover-the-offer) picks up there, because consent UI has the same duty: stay out of the sentence the visitor came to read.
